turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gary, come through. You look wiped. How's the diabetes been going?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Shocking. I'm tired, and the sugars are all over the place.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tired how?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I could put my head on the bench and be gone. Weeks of it. And yeah, I'm snappy, I know.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): What are the meter readings doing?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting's one-eighty-something. Sometimes it flashes two hundred and I just stop looking. I don't write them down.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Did you see the cricket last night? Covers came on after about twelve overs, Smith poking at everything, and then it just rained.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): I caught the highlights. Grim night for a game.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Then the West Gate was a car park. Prang near the Altona exit, forty minutes of brake lights, radio still going on about the rain. Nearly turned around.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Miserable in that weather. Any thirst, or up at night passing urine?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Thirsty all day. Up twice a night for a wee. Same sort of stretch, weeks.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the eyes, any change in the vision?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Blurry first thing in the morning. Settles once I've had a coffee. I can still see to drive.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain or shortness of breath?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Chest is fine. I'm just—
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry. The feet. Numbness, sores, any pain?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Toes go tingly at night, both feet, like pins and... yeah. No sores. I look, mostly.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did the tingling start?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Work's been six-day weeks. That's half of why I'm wrecked.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): The tingling, though.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. A couple of months, I s'pose. Not sure of the exact week. It crept up.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Still on the metformin?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Thousand milligrams by mouth, twice a day, with meals. For the diabetes. That one I do take.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): And gliclazide?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Sixty milligrams by mouth in the morning. Work days I skip it. Early starts, don't want a hypo on the tools.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): So you're missing it several days a week.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Four, sometimes five. Don't start on me.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): The nurse's med rec this morning has Lantus, twenty-six units at night.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): She's wrong. I draw up eighteen units at bedtime. Eighteen since they cut it. Twenty-six was ages ago.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Eighteen from you, twenty-six from her. What about the Ozempic?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Stopped that in March. Made me throw up. Not a dose since.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the Forxiga, dapagliflozin, the script we did?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Never took it. Still in the glove box. Not one tablet.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. Nothing.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did your dad have diabetes?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Type two, yeah. And a heart attack at sixty-eight.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Still carpentry?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Carpentry, on the tools, and it's still six-day weeks. Never smoked. A beer of a Saturday, that's all the drinking.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have you had the diabetes?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Twelve years, type two. Blood pressure's been up for years too. Ramipril five milligrams by mouth every morning for that.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shoes off. I'll have a look at the feet.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Give us a sec with these boots.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Skin's intact, no ulcers. Pulses present in both feet. Sensation is dull over the toes, left and right.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nurse recorded blood pressure one forty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-eight, and weight ninety-four kilos.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Saying it back. Twelve years of type two, blood pressure up for years, weeks of tiredness and thirst, up twice a night, blurry mornings, tingling both feet for a couple of months you can't pin to a week.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. I'm over it.

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Metformin a thousand milligrams twice a day, gliclazide sixty skipped on work days, Lantus eighteen by your count and twenty-six on the nurse's note, ramipril five each morning. Ozempic off since March. No chest pain, no breathlessness, no foot sores, no drug allergies.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thirst and tiredness fit the glucose running high. How high, I won't know till the bloods. The toe tingling could be early neuropathy, and I'm not calling that yet.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): I was going to lift the Lantus to twenty-two units and refer you across to endocrine.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Don't. We don't even agree the dose, and I skip that morning tablet. You'll flatten me on the site.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Point taken. Scratch the increase and hold the referral. No change to the insulin today, and no new tablet.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will send an HbA1c, a urine albumin-creatinine ratio, and a fasting lipid panel. Have them done on the way out.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Bloods, yeah, fine.

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in four weeks with a written diary of the actual meter numbers, not one-eighty-something. Take the gliclazide on work days with breakfast, and don't skip the Lantus.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks. If I hypo out there I'll be ropeable.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep a sandwich in the ute. If you feel shaky, stop and check the sugar before you carry on.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the tingling gets worse, or you spot a sore on either foot, come back sooner rather than waiting.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): The eyes, since you asked. Last proper test, I can't date it. Maybe twenty twenty-two, or maybe that wasn't it. No idea.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Book an optometrist when you can. I'm not ordering retinal photos from here.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations in the past, appendix or otherwise?
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never been under the knife.
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Bloods today, leave the Lantus wherever it truly sits until eighteen versus twenty-six is sorted, and I'll see you in four weeks.

spec.situation: Type 2 diabetic on tablets plus insulin; patient and nurse give different insulin doses, patient skips doses on work days, reads home sugar numbers aloud in a muddled way ('one-eighty-something fasting'). Foot and eye questions.
features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

omissions.text: Home glucose readings were reported as fasting around 180 mg/dL, sometimes 200 mg/dL, and the patient does not record them.
Gliclazide adherence detail is more specific: the patient skips it on work days because of fear of a hypo on the tools, about 4 to 5 days per week.
Lantus dose detail is missing from the medication list: the patient reports 18 units at bedtime, and says 26 units was an old dose.
Ozempic discontinuation reason and timing detail are missing: stopped in March because it made him vomit, with no dose since.
Forxiga (dapagliflozin) was prescribed but never started; the patient says the tablets are still in the glove box and he has taken not one tablet.

The patient denied numbness and foot pain only indirectly by reporting tingling and specifically denying sores; numbness and pain were asked about but not explicitly answered, so they should not be inferred as negative findings.
A planned insulin increase to Lantus 22 units and a referral to endocrinology were discussed, but then canceled after the patient's objection.
Plan detail: no change to insulin today and no new tablet.
Instruction on timing of labs is missing: HbA1c, urine albumin-creatinine ratio, and fasting lipid panel were to be done on the way out / bloods today.
Follow-up plan included leaving the Lantus dose unchanged wherever it truly sits until the 18-versus-26-unit discrepancy is sorted.
